s11.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:30 PM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — THE PITCH
s11.music: Talking Heads — “This Must Be the Place (Naive Melody)”
body: At one o’clock Hale went on with “The Dead,” as far as Gabriel’s speech, and called on neither of them. Lena sat at the far end of the oak table and wrote steadily, and at ten to two it was over.

The afternoon comes through the one window flat and white off the ridge behind Engineering, and by half past three 412 has been turned into an office. Theo’s desk is cleared to the grain, the MacBook shut, the blazer hung on the chair back, and the little speakers on the sill are playing a song Jack knows without being able to name: a jumpy guitar, a bass line that lets itself in and sits on the furniture, a nervous tenor trying to make friends. Theo stands in the middle of the floor in his shirtsleeves, the cuffs turned back twice, and waits for the door to close behind Jack.
“Sit,” he says. “It’s a pitch. The buyer sits.”
“I live here.”
“Then you know where the bed is.”
Jack sits on his bed with the bag still on his shoulder and opens his mouth.
“No. You may speak at the end. It’s in the contract.”
“There’s a contract?”
“There is a contract the moment I stand up, Costigan. It’s why I stand up.” Theo draws a rectangle in the air, corner to corner, with one finger, and taps the place where the title would go.

“Fade in,” he says. “New Orleans. Sunday night, the seventh of February, kickoff at twenty-five past five, local, the hour the light on the river goes gold. A city that has waited forty-three years for its football team to be good has just been told it can stop waiting. The Colts are favored by six, and the city does not believe in six. Every bar in the Quarter will have a priest in it, and he will be winning.” He taps the air. “The franchise was awarded on All Saints’ Day, Costigan. I looked it up. Your feast, your people, your game.”

“Logline. A football kid from a football town, who has spent every autumn of his life in a Youngstown garage being told that next year is next year, is offered the one night in history when somebody else’s next year arrives. And elects to watch it in the Fishbowl.” Another tap. “With Doug. Doug will bring a diagram. The diagram will be wrong.”
“Doug’s diagrams have a Sasquatch in them.”
“Then the Sasquatch is in the Fishbowl, and you are in the Quarter.”

“Your father has been waiting on Cleveland all his life,” he goes on, more quietly, and then catches himself and puts the volume back on. “Here is a city whose wait is over, offering to let you stand next to it while it finds out. Cast.” He ticks it off across the air, left to right. “Kevin, as Caution. Margot, as Science. Laney, as Weather.”
“And you?”
“I’m the producer. Producers are never in the picture, Costigan. It’s the great tragedy of the form.”
“Who plays me?”
“You play you. It’s a documentary.” The hand comes down. “You walked out of Sully’s for a girl. Walk back in for a city.”
It is a good speech, and Jack wants it: the Quarter on a Sunday night, a city coming apart in gold. He is also already holding the no.

choices.text: “The game’s in Miami. You’re pitching me a bar.”
response: Theo brightens. “A bar the size of a city, with a river in it.” Miami has a stadium, he allows; New Orleans has the *game*, and those are different products, Costigan, because one of them is a building. He nods the geography through and goes on exactly as before. Jack has the point and can’t find where to spend it.

choices.text: “I’m a Browns fan. ‘Once in a lifetime’ is what they say to us so we’ll renew.”
response: Theo laughs, a bark that is not in the pitch, and has to wipe the board off the air with his forearm to find his place. “Cleveland has been renewing since 1964,” he says. “I see what you did there. I’m going to need to see it again, slowly, from the other side.”
“He admits it,” Theo says. “Let the minutes show it.”
“Still no,” Jack says.
Theo writes STILL NO on the air in block capitals, underlines it twice, and moves on to the next board, visibly pleased and not about to waste it.

s11a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:41 PM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — THE PITCH
body: Theo wipes the first board off the air with his forearm and starts a second, lower and to the left, and the speech changes gear from trailer to timetable.
“Item,” he says. “Transportation. Kevin’s mother has lent us the Odyssey: seven seats for six people and a cooler, assigned by Kevin in a seating chart. It has a legend, Costigan. It has a *key*.”
“Kevin made a legend.”
“Kevin made two. One is for the glovebox.”

“Item. Gas, split six ways. Sixty-one dollars a head. Item. Lodging. Celeste Broussard has made up an attic with four mattresses and a ghost, who is, I’m told, a Saints fan, and a front room for whoever loses the coin toss. Item. Gloria loves a pilgrimage. Her words, Tuesday, by the pie case.”
“You asked Gloria.”

“I consulted Gloria. She said *hon* in several keys and then she said yes. Item. Music. Kevin has submitted a playlist. It is called *Road Trip Mix* and contains nothing recorded after 1987 and two by the Carpenters, and I have decided to admire it. Item. Kevin will drive at sixty-five. Not sixty-six. He says sixty-six is a lifestyle. Item. Margot has asked that we call the trip a field season. Item. Laney has packed for us, individually, in labeled bags. Mine says *Mr. Theodore, Medium Sparkle*. I haven’t opened it. I’m afraid of what it knows.”
“What does mine say?”
“*Costigan, Large.* Nothing else. She is extremely angry with you and extremely thorough.”

“Item. Hale.” Theo lifts his chin. “He will excuse you for an essay. I have it on authority. ‘Mr. Costigan may go, provided he writes me four thousand words on the theology of the second line, and not one of them *liminal*.’” The second line, he explains, is everyone who dances behind the band on the way home from the cemetery. “I understand it is very nearly your entire position.”
It is, annoyingly, an essay Jack would like to write. He has the first sentence before he can stop himself: the band goes out slow and comes back loose.

response: Theo gets specific, the way Theo does when there is nothing under it. It was Monday, in the corridor outside 302, at ten past three, Hale in the green tie with the soup on it and the dog asleep on his left foot.
“Berkeley’s blanket was empty Monday,” Jack says. “I was in the room. You made that up.”
“I *anticipated* it,” Theo says.

choices.text: “Sixty-one dollars. You did math. You’ve never done math.”
response: “I had it done,” Theo says. “By Margot. For science.”
“Does she bill by the hour?”
“By the footnote. I have been told there are eleven.”

choices.text: “Kevin’s mother would let me drive the Odyssey?”
response: “Kevin’s mother asked for you by name,” Theo says. He says it flat, with nothing hung on it, no day of the week, no pie case, no legend, and goes straight on to the next item before Jack can say anything to it.

s11b.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:50 PM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — THE PITCH
body: The song ends, and the next one doesn’t start; the speakers hold the room with a little hiss in it. Down in the lot somebody is trying to start a Corolla, and failing with a great deal of heart. Theo has wiped the second board off the air and draws no third. He stands in the middle of the floor with his hands at his sides. Jack has not seen them do that before.
The voice that sells is gone. What is left is lower and has less in it.
“I need you there,” Theo says.

In five months Theo has put a cashmere on him, lent him a Burberry in a storm, dressed him for the Palisades in a charcoal suit pinned to fit, covered for him at the fire alarm, and walked into Hale’s house with a bottle that had a story. He has never asked for anything back. He has not asked for this, either, in any way Jack can find to turn down. He has only said it, and given no reason, and stayed where he is. Theo lies by adding furniture. This has none. Jack goes for the joke where he keeps it, and it isn’t there.

response: Theo gives him a reason. It runs to a full minute and has everything in it: Laney, who has the gas card and the schedule; Margot, who has printed the maps in three colors and will be unbearable if they go unused; a hotel in Beaumont, Texas, with a waffle iron in the lobby that Theo has seen a photograph of and believes in. Jack lets him finish. At the end of it Theo says, low and level and with no waffle in it, “Because I asked.”
“Don’t get used to it,” Theo says. He turns to the speakers and brings the music back up a notch past where it was, and stays with his back to the room until the track has gotten somewhere.

choices.text: “You’ve been on her side all month, Theo. Don’t pitch me her trip.”
response: It lands; Jack can watch it land. Monday’s corridor comes back to him, and what Hale said in it, and he has gone and done it anyway. Theo takes it with a nod at the rug, and for a moment there is nothing on the board at all.

response.text: “You told me it’s love,” Theo says. “I believed you. This isn’t about that.”

s11c.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:58 PM · DELGADO HALL, 412 — THE NO

body.text: Theo looks at his empty air-board. “You won,” he says. “The points, anyway. I want that noted somewhere official.”
Theo looks at his empty air-board. “You agreed with everything I said,” he says. “That’s worse.”
Theo looks at his empty air-board. “You were funny,” he says. “Funny isn’t the same as right. You taught me that.”

body: “And you’re going to say no anyway.”
“No,” Jack says. It comes out as level and easy as the time of day.
“I have a slide for this.”
“There aren’t any slides.”
“There is a slide, Costigan. It’s on the other board.” Theo regards the air where it would be. “It says *Reconsider*. In a font.” He folds his arms. “Give me the reason. I’m owed a reason.”
Twenty-eight minutes of Theo’s afternoon have gone into this: a cleared desk, a speech with a priest in it, a legend on a seating chart. Whatever Jack says next had better be the right size.

choices.text: “Thirty hours in a van with Lena Broussard. Ten days in her mother’s house. I’m not doing that to Skye, and I’m not doing it to me.”
choices.key: Theo pitched New Orleans — the Saints, the money, and for the first time in his life a favor. You said no: thirty hours in a van with Lena, and you’re not doing that to Skye.
response: Theo takes it standing up, with his chin level. He draws one last board in the air, a small one, writes nothing on it, and folds it in half and in half again and puts it in his shirt pocket. “I’ll put you down as a maybe,” he says.
He takes the blazer off the chair, and at the door he stops with a hand on the frame. “Ask her.”
“Ask who?”
“Whoever you ask,” Theo says. His shoes go off down the hall toward the elevator.
Jack sits on his bed with the bag still on his shoulder, in a room rearranged for the sole purpose of asking him something, and takes the bag off.

choices.key: Theo pitched New Orleans — the Saints, the money, and for the first time in his life a favor. You said no, because you don’t want to.
response: Theo looks at him. “That’s the first lie you’ve told me since August,” he says.

Jack has no reply, and Theo seems to have expected none. He pinches the last board out of the air and puts it in his pocket, and by the time he says “I’ll put you down as a no I didn’t hear” he is in the hall with the blazer over his arm.
“Ask her,” comes back through the doorway.
“Ask who?”
“Whoever you ask,” says the hall.
Through the wall Doug says *dude* to a screen, and the song runs out into the next one.

choices.text: “Because Kevin drives like the Rapture’s at the next exit and he wants to be found doing the speed limit. And her.”
choices.key: Theo pitched New Orleans — the Saints, the money, and for the first time in his life a favor. You made a joke about Kevin’s driving, and then said the real reason: her.
response: Theo has the blazer off the chair and is working his arms into it when Jack reaches the second half, and one arm stays in its sleeve. “The second part was the pitch,” he says. “I’ll put you down as pending.”
He gets the other arm in. At the mirror on the back of the door he squares the Sigma Rho pin on his lapel. “Ask her.”
“Ask who?”
“Whoever you ask.”
In the mirror Jack watches Theo’s face for whatever it is doing, and it is entirely occupied with the pin.

body: The east stairwell has one bulb, a Spring Rush poster, and a landing where the cold comes up from the loading dock. Jack sits on the fourth step with the RAZR open in both hands. Theo is forty feet away behind a door that doesn’t lock, and it seems important that this go through a carrier.
Priya comes up from the third floor on her rounds with a flashlight she does not need, in a stairwell with a bulb, and stops two steps below him.
“The stairwell is for egress,” she says. “It is not a lounge.”
“I’m egressing.”
“You’re composing.” She puts the flashlight on the phone, courteously, and then on the ceiling, and goes up past him. “I’m not going to say anything. I’m going to remember it.”

body: He sends it. Nothing comes back, and he hadn’t wanted anything to.

412 is dark but for the streetlight, which comes through the one window in a long orange block and lies across Theo’s bed. Theo is in it in his shirt, facing the wall, the blanket pulled to his ear, and over his empty desk Rosie’s princes have their crayon crowns lit. On the nightstand there is a pale ring in the veneer the width of a teacup, and no teacup. Jack gets the door to without the click and has one shoe off when the wall speaks.
“Kevin drives the first shift,” Theo says. “You drive West Texas.”
“Who decided that?”
“There’s a chart.”

He doesn’t turn over. He laughs, quietly, into the pillow: a breath through the nose, and then a second one behind it. On the nightstand, in the pale ring, his iPhone lights face-up with a text Jack can’t read from here, and the glow slides across the ceiling and fades.
Jack gets the other shoe off and lies down in his clothes.

body.text: On the desk, standing in its coffee mug, unlit, is her Candlemas candle, the wax gone white down one side where it ran over her thumb.
body.else: On the desk, standing in its coffee mug, unlit, is his Candlemas candle, the one he is keeping for Nonna.

body: Across the room Theo’s breathing has gone slow and even a good deal faster than anyone falls asleep. Jack lies on his back with his shoes on the floor and looks at the candle until the wick, a small dark stroke at the top of it, is the only part he can see.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it. Christmas: called from LA to ask for Christmas Eve and Christmas Day. I answered on the first ring; he sounded surprised. Dad said he doesn’t have to call first. Wore the parka again. Ma glued his name on a stocking. Nonna has his cashmere. Ate an eel. Took my phone out of Rosie’s hand at dinner and gave it to me face-down. Christmas Eve he came with me to Trumbull, bought from the machines, and did Dad for Danny. Danny asked him who comes to see him. He said I do. Danny says he’s on the list for good. Wears the Browns hat now. Laney has a schedule. Landed in the middle of the night — they wanded the baccalà in Pittsburgh. At the side door Christmas afternoon he said, Be careful, Costigan. Of what. All of it. New Year’s Eve, at nine his time, the party was already a disappointment. Wore Ma’s scarf in sixty-one degrees. A woman asked if he was in a band. Back from LA in the orange hat and Ma’s scarf. Says the hat is a family heirloom. Sunday night: ‘Congratulations, Costigan.’ ‘Go to sleep. Monday is going to be a long day.’ Tuesday morning he did the responses too: Lord, hear our prayer. Rushing Sigma Rho; ate a raw onion in front of the lacrosse team. Wednesday night he got a bid. A pledge now. Carries a raw egg named Hollis in a teacup; if it breaks, he’s out. At Sully’s: ‘She’s the best actress I know, Costigan. Never ask her if she’s acting.’ MLK Day he shoveled sand one-handed for Sigma Rho with Hollis in the other. At midnight Wednesday he pitched me a movie about a man whose friend got dumped and was with somebody else in a week. He said it twice. Hollis made his week. Theo’s in. He’s keeping the egg. Saturday he became a brother. Sunday he runs. He was correct to Lena for seven hours at Sully’s and sent me the end of it. He started on Julian, and I told him to stop. Monday he asked me, hypothetically, where a man who doesn’t go to Sully’s watches the Super Bowl. Made himself my plus-one to Hale’s, with a bottle that had a story. Tuesday morning I told him I think she’s the answer. He wanted a pamphlet, framed. Then he said nobody ever asked her to be that, and an answer is heavy for the person you hand it to. At Hale’s door Laney told him that wasn’t about a book. He said no. At midnight, to the ceiling: don’t ever make me watch that again. Thursday he dressed me for the Palisades: his charcoal suit, pinned, and a half-Windsor — a commitment, like a coat. In the mirror he said I was good at it Wednesday, and that’s what he didn’t like. Friday: “You stayed.” She kept me there. “That’s love.” Saturday I tied his for the Pi Lam formal. He wanted the January call word for word. I gave it to him once. He asked if I know what I’m going to say tomorrow, if she asks. Monday: six days. Hollis was concerned; he told him I’d been detained by the Holy See. Monday night, two legal pads with Laney: a wedding seating chart, hypothetical. Tuesday he spent the night at the house and left me the room. Wednesday he pitched me New Orleans like a movie — the Saints, the money, and then, for the first time since I’ve known him, a favor. I need you there. I said no. That night I said yes, by text, from the stairs. Kevin drives the first shift. I drive West Texas.
